bib.title: When is Routing Meaningful? Diversity and Robustness in Language Model Societies

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "When is Routing Meaningful? Diversity and Robustness in Language Model Societies", Fantine Huot, Michael Kaisers, Mirella Lapata (Google DeepMind). arXiv 2607.09197v1 [cs.MA], 10 Jul 2026. Preprint (no venue printed).
COVERAGE: 68,481 of 68,481 chars read (main text, limitations, appendices A-F, Fig 7 caption start). Last ~1k chars (rest of Fig 7 caption) were not displayed; nothing else skipped. Figures not rendered, only captions from the text.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Routing can be "meaningless" even at high accuracy: the paper says a society must be behaviourally differentiated and the router must be stable under surface-form variants.
 number: none (framing)
 setup: conceptual; metrics HSE (diversity) and rho (robustness).
 quote: "High task accuracy is compatible with violating both properties, since a router can operate over a redundant society or assign queries inconsistently, preventing specialisation regardless of performance."
 where: Abstract
2. A curated subset of fewer than ten agents recovers most diversity in a large pool (strong diminishing returns).
 number: 9 of 112 models (EmbedLLM); 4 of 11 (RouterBench)
 setup: normalised HSE, cosine distance, single linkage, greedy selection. Actors are models with binary-correctness behavioural vectors. EmbedLLM: 112 models, 36,054 questions, 10 benchmarks. RouterBench: 11 models, 36,497 queries, 8 datasets.
 quote: "fewer than ten agents suffice to capture most available diversity in EmbedLLM, and four agents in RouterBench"
 where: Sec 1; Fig 3; App A.1-A.2
3. Real-world model pools are less diverse than purpose-built specialists of similar size. Size alone does not imply diversity.
 number: HSE 1.62 (default 112 models) vs 2.32 (RD, 5 experts), 3.19 (RD+SA, 20), 3.91 (SA, 15)
 setup: EmbedLLM; synthetic experts have binary 0/1 profiles by construction, oracle accuracy 1.0.
 quote: "The SA society (HSE = 3.91) is more than twice as diverse as the default (HSE = 1.62)"
 where: Sec 6-7
4. KNN routers gain clean accuracy on specialist societies but collapse in robustness. The prompted (LLM) router stays stable.
 number: perturbed KNN accuracy "near-random"; prompted clean-vs-perturbed gap "less than five points" on SA
 setup: EmbedLLM; routers: random, prompted (Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite, 4 few-shot exemplars per actor, margin 0.4), KNN-1/3/10 (Gemini Embedding 2). 5 perturbations per query, one per level.
 quote: "Its clean accuracy on SA is lower than KNN-10, but perturbed accuracy remains close, a gap of less than five points. Crucially, robustness rises monotonically with HSE"
 where: Sec 7, Fig 4
5. Max-HSE subsets improve prompted-router robustness. KNN gains are pool-dependent: large on RouterBench, mixed on EmbedLLM, where KNN-1 gets worse.
 number: rho 0.24 -> 0.53 (EmbedLLM), 0.26 -> 0.44 (RouterBench). These are the axis labels in Fig 5, and the text does not say which router they refer to. The text says the prompted router "roughly" doubles on EmbedLLM.
 quote: "The prompted router improves consistently, roughly doubling its robustness on EmbedLLM and improving more modestly on RouterBench."
 where: Sec 7, Fig 5. Do not cite 0.24/0.53 as the prompted router's rho. Those figures are probably the normalised HSE of the default and max-HSE societies (Table 7 shows "default 0.24, HSE 9 0.53").
6. Robustness is roughly flat across the five perturbation levels. Paraphrase is no worse than typos.
 number: prompted rho 0.589 (paraphrase) to 0.617 (syntax) on the full RouterBench society; 0.663 to 0.744 on the max-HSE subset.
 quote: "the prompted router ranges from 0.589 (paraphrase) to 0.617 (syntax) on the full society, and from 0.663 (para-phrase) to 0.744 (word) on the max-HSE subset."
 where: Sec 7, Fig 6
7. Diversity versus accuracy trade-off in subset selection: HSE-only subsets lose routing accuracy, and adding accuracy to the criterion recovers it.
 number: at n=9, KNN-10 accuracy 0.65 (same as the full 112-model society); oracle 0.92; normalised HSE 0.48 vs 0.53.
 setup: EmbedLLM; Table 7. HSE-only n=9: KNN-10 0.46, oracle 0.87. Full 112-model society: KNN-10 0.65, oracle 0.97.
 quote: "at n= 9, KNN-10 matches the full 112-model society exactly (0.65) and oracle reaches 0.92 — but at the cost of lower HSE (0.48 vs. 0.53)."
 where: App F
8. HSE sanity checks: identical actors give HSE 0; orthogonal actors give normalised 1.0; duplicating a model or a prompt does not inflate HSE.
 number: 0.0 and 1.585 (raw, 3 orthogonal actors)
 where: Tables 1-2
Metric definitions
 - rho_i is the fraction of p perturbations routed to the same actor as the original.
 - A fixed router has rho = 1; a uniform random router has E[rho] = 1/N.
 - Five perturbation levels: character, word, syntax, paraphrase, rambling.

LIMITS
 - Authors concede HSE depends on a representative evaluation set E.
 - Greedy subset selection is not guaranteed optimal.
 - Synthetic societies have binary profiles and oracle accuracy 1.0, so "the KNN brittleness we observe may be attenuated in practice."
 - Single-turn queries only. Stable routing is necessary, not shown sufficient, for specialisation. The paper does not test whether actors actually specialise.
 - The authors say multi-step agentic settings are future work. It does not test supervisor/router topologies in agent graphs or prompt-vs-model-per-node specialisation, and it has no end-to-end task-quality results.
 - Actors are mostly different models. The paper says actors can be prompts, tools or roles, but its experiments use model pools and synthetic experts. Its claim that diversity is measurable for same-backbone, different-prompt societies is conceptual only (Sec 3).
 - The prompted router uses a single backbone (Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite) and the KNN uses Gemini Embedding 2. The paper does not vary these.
 - Models are dated: RouterBench uses GPT-4, Claude-v1/v2, Llama-70B-chat and similar.
 - No variance or seed information is given in the text.
 - The authors do not claim diversity is always desirable ("homogeneous teams may outperform diverse ones").
 For your target note: the paper does not directly support "specialise by prompt first". It gives a related measurable argument: many real models are behaviourally redundant, so a router over them can be vacuous. Use it as supporting evidence for measuring before adding models per node, not as a test of prompt-vs-model specialisation.

BUILDS ON
 - Balch (2000), Hierarchic Social Entropy, Autonomous Robots 8(3).
 - Bettini, Shankar, Prorok (2025), System Neural Diversity, JMLR 26(163).
 - Stanley et al. (2019) (behaviour vs parameter space).
 - Sclar et al. (2024) (prompt-format sensitivity).
 - Labella et al. (2006); Nitschke et al. (2008) (specialisation in robots).
 - Krogh and Vedelsby (1994); Mouret and Clune (2015).
 - Benchmarks: EmbedLLM (Zhuang et al., ICLR 2025), RouterBench (Hu et al., ICML 2024 Workshop on Agentic Markets).
 - Routing context: FrugalGPT (Chen, Zaharia, Zou, TMLR 2024), RouteLLM (Ong et al., 2025), MasRouter (Yue et al., 2025).
 - Multi-agent frameworks: Wu et al. 2024; Hong et al. 2024 (MetaGPT); Li et al. 2023.

CODE: none. The prompt template (App C.1) is "Given a prompt, select which model is best positioned to answer. Your answer should be one of:{actors}." with actor descriptions, few-shot exemplars, and "Best model for this prompt:".

FIGURES: the best candidate is Fig 4 (p. 7): "Task accuracy (a) and robustness rho (b) across EmbedLLM societies ordered by HSE. Solid lines show original queries; dashed lines in (a) show perturbations. KNN routers gain accuracy on specialist societies but lose robustness; the prompted router maintains both." It shows accuracy and robustness diverging in a single plot. Fig 3 (p. 7) shows the diminishing-returns curve.

PROBLEMS: There is no extraction fault in the text. Figure and table numbers (Fig 5 axis labels) were read from text only, so some values are ambiguous (see claim 5). The paper's text has no embedded instructions.
